title: The Nagpur Mill Bombay Laughed At, and the Machinery Tata Scrapped
dek: In the 1870s Jamsetji Tata built a cotton mill near the cotton fields instead of in Bombay, then had to undo his own decision to buy cheap machinery.

story.event: Choosing Nagpur over Bombay for a cotton mill, then replacing the cheap machinery that nearly sank it
story.summary: In the mid-1870s Jamsetji Tata chose Nagpur, in cotton country with rail and coal nearby, for a new cotton mill instead of Bombay, and in 1874 formed the Central India Spinning, Weaving and Manufacturing Company. The Empress Mills opened on 1 January 1877, but cheap machinery bought to save capital gave poor yarn and the shares fell to half their value; Tata bought new plant in 1878 and the company paid a 16 per cent dividend in 1881.
paragraphs: On 26 April 1873 Jamsetji Tata, then 34, left Bombay on a journey to Lancashire, to study the cotton trade and its newest machinery. He had just sold the Alexandra Mill, a converted Bombay property he had run at a moderate profit, and wanted something bigger. Bombay's mill-owners held that Bombay alone was the place to build. Tata, his biographer Frank Harris wrote in 1925, saw that the city was far from the districts where cotton grew, and wanted a site near the raw material and a market, with coal and water to hand.

Following a suggestion of his father's, he toured likely districts. His first choice, Jubbulpore, where the Narmada's falls could have powered the mill, fell through when officials refused the concession, fearing a riot over a fakir's shrine there. He settled on Nagpur, some 500 miles from Bombay: in cotton country, at the end of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, within reach of coal from the Warora mines. Bombay, Harris wrote, “laughed him to scorn.” In 1874 he, his father and a few friends formed the Central India Spinning, Weaving and Manufacturing Company, with Rs 15 lakh of capital.

The land he bought, near the railway station, was marshy ground beside an old reservoir, which he had levelled with earth from nearby mounds. One local banker refused to buy shares in a man putting “gold into the ground.” The mill opened on 1 January 1877, the day Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India, and Tata named it the Empress Mills.

Then came the setback. To conserve capital, Tata had bought a cheaper class of machinery in England. The yarn was poor, output was low and, Harris wrote, the shares fell to half their nominal value; a fire in the loom shed made things worse. In 1878 Tata went back to England and bought new plant, this time paying for efficiency over economy. He had also hired Bezonji Dadabhai Mehta, a railway goods superintendent who knew nothing of cotton, and trained him to run the mill.

In 1881 the company paid a 16 per cent dividend, and over the following years the cheaper machinery was scrapped shop by shop. The banker, Harris recorded, later admitted that Tata had “put in earth, and had taken out gold.”

quote.text: Do nothing without counsel; and when thou hast once done, repent not.
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira advises taking counsel and then not looking back. Tata kept half of that: he never wavered over Nagpur, however Bombay laughed. But what rescued the mill was a decision already made and paid for that he did regret, and reversed within about a year.

reflection: Tata held to one decision and undid another, and the difference was not stubbornness. His reasons for Nagpur were still true after Bombay laughed: the cotton, the railway and the coal had not moved. His reason for the cheap machinery, saving money, had been answered by poor yarn and falling shares. He let the evidence decide which choice to defend.

You will have choices you argued for in public and smaller ones that are quietly failing. Pride tends to guard both the same way. It can help to ask of each what it was meant to achieve and whether it still is, before asking whether you were right.
invitation: Name one thing you chose mainly because it was cheaper. Ask honestly whether it now costs you more in time or worry than it saved, and if it does, write down what replacing it would take.

research_notes: Dates of company formation: Harris (1925) says Tata began promoting the Central India Spinning, Weaving and Manufacturing Company in 1874; the Encyclopedia of World Biography entry says 1871. The story uses Harris, whose account is detailed and dated. Capital: Harris gives Rs 15,00,000 (3,000 shares of Rs 500); a search-engine summary of other pages gave Rs 1.5 lakh, which does not match Harris and was not used. The machinery mistake, the shares at half nominal value, the loom-shed fire, the 1878 purchase of new plant and the 1881 dividend of 16 per cent rest on Harris alone (the tata.com page is an excerpt of Harris; the archive.org text is the same book), so they are attributed to him in the story; Wacha (1914) independently records only that early working had many difficulties to surmount. The Jubbulpore episode: Harris says the concession was refused over fears of a riot about a fakir's shrine; Wacha mentions only that Tata looked for a site near the Jubbulpore marble falls. The banker's 'gold into the ground' anecdote is Harris's. Age: born 3 March 1839 (Encyclopedia of World Biography), so 34 on 26 April 1873; Wacha says the mill opened in the thirty-eighth year of his life. Harris writes of Tata's 'visit to England' for the machinery; the 1873 journey went via Egypt, Palestine, Turkey and Russia. Funding is set to 'mixed': the company's capital came from Tata, his father and a small number of outside subscribers. Ben Sira's maxim is general advice on counsel and resolve, applied by analogy; the edition is the 1910 Wisdom of the East selection, which follows the Revised Version wording. A separate edition covers J. R. D. Tata's 1932 airmail flight, a different founder and episode.
